【対象Topic】
A longitudinal study of parent–child relationship and behavioral problems in children aged 3 to 6: the mediating role of screen time
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1794353/full

【一次Sourceの抽出テキスト(Claude Codeがこの既知URLへ直接アクセスして取得したもの、
Web検索結果ではない)】
Full Title: A longitudinal study of parent-child relationship and behavioral problems in children aged 3 to 6: the mediating role of screen time
Authors: Xiaojun Ling, Mengqi Li, Jiahui Sun
Journal: Frontiers in Psychology, Section: Media Psychology, Volume 17, 2026
DOI: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1794353
Publication Date: May 25, 2026

Study Design: Longitudinal with three assessment waves spaced 4 months apart.
Sample Size: 532 valid cases (initial recruitment n=619; attrition of 87 participants, 14.1%).
Participant Age: Children aged 3 to 6 years (mean age 3.99 years, SD=0.85). Age breakdown: 198 children age 3 (37.2%), 150 age 4 (28.2%), 184 age 5 (34.6%); 289 boys (54.3%), 243 girls (45.7%).
Country/Population: Fuyang City, Anhui Province, China; data collected via Wenjuanxing platform; all respondents were mothers.
Time Points: Three waves (T1, T2, T3), 4 months apart.

Measurement - Parent-Child Relationship: Child-Parent Relationship Scale (CPRS), Chinese revised version by Deng (2013). Two subscales: Closeness (7 items, alpha=0.882) and Conflict (8 items, alpha=0.895). Five-point Likert scale (1=not at all true to 5=completely true).
Measurement - Screen Time: Two items measuring average daily electronic device use on weekdays and weekends; weighted average = (weekday average x 5 + weekend average x 2)/7.
Measurement - Behavioral Problems: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Externalizing problems (alpha=0.891) via Hyperactivity/Inattention and Conduct Problems subscales (5 items each). Internalizing problems (alpha=0.853) via Emotional Symptoms and Peer Problems subscales (5 items each). Three-point scale (1=not true to 3=certainly true).

Main Statistical Results:
Conflictual parent-child relationship (T1) -> Internalizing behavioral problems (T3): beta=0.476, p<0.001, 95% CI [0.302, 0.650]
Conflictual parent-child relationship (T1) -> Externalizing behavioral problems (T3): beta=0.273, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.118, 0.428]
Conflictual parent-child relationship (T1) -> Screen time (T2): beta=0.208, p<0.001, 95% CI [0.094, 0.322]
Screen time (T2) -> Internalizing problems (T3): beta=0.148, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.011, 0.285]
Screen time (T2) -> Externalizing problems (T3): beta=0.149, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.016, 0.282]
Indirect effect Conflict -> Screen time -> Internalizing: beta=0.031, p<0.05, 95% CI [-0.026, 0.088]
Indirect effect Conflict -> Screen time -> Externalizing: beta=0.031, p<0.05, 95% CI [-0.022, 0.084]
Close parent-child relationship (T1) -> Screen time (T2): beta=0.006, p>0.05 (not significant), 95% CI [-0.088, 0.100]
Close parent-child relationship (T1) -> Internalizing problems (T3): beta=-0.157, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.294, -0.020]
Close parent-child relationship (T1) -> Externalizing problems (T3): beta=-0.213, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.346, -0.080]
Indirect effects of Close relationship via screen time: not significant for either internalizing or externalizing problems.

Model fit: chi2(7)=19.27, p<0.05; RMSEA=0.057, 90% CI [0.028, 0.089]; CFI=0.950; TLI=0.917; SRMR=0.028.

Stated Limitations (verbatim from authors):
- The present study did not include baseline levels of key variables, which may have resulted in insufficient control for stable between-person differences at initial assessment. As a consequence, some of the observed indirect effects may partially reflect pre-existing levels of the constructs rather than purely developmental processes.
- The screen time measure does not capture important contextual information that may be critical for understanding its role in child development.
- All core variables in the present study were reported by a single informant; reliance on a single source of information remains a methodological limitation.
- The study captures only a limited developmental time window. The relatively short measurement interval may not adequately reflect the dynamic interplay among screen time, parent-child relationships, and behavioral problems over time. Accordingly, the generalizability of the findings across longer developmental periods should be interpreted with caution.
- The association between parent-child relationships and children behavioral outcomes does not necessarily operate directly through screen time; underlying mechanisms are likely more complex, potentially involving indirect pathways through other mediating or moderating processes.
- Although participants were recruited through kindergartens and classes, the present study did not explicitly model the nested data structure (e.g., children within classes or schools). Thus, potential clustering effects cannot be entirely ruled out.
- Caution is warranted when interpreting the causal implications of the observed mediating effects.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Participants were children aged 3 to 6 years, with a mean age of 3.99 years (SD=0.85). The age distribution was 198 three-year-olds (37.2%), 150 four-year-olds (28.2%), and 184 five-year-olds (34.6%). The sample included 289 boys (54.3%) and 243 girls (45.7%).
evidence_items.numeric_value: Mean age 3.99 years, SD=0.85; age counts 198, 150, and 184; 289 boys and 243 girls
evidence_items.numeric_scope: 532 valid cases
evidence_items.population: Children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Descriptive participant characteristics only.
evidence_items.limitation: Although the stated target range is 3 to 6 years, the reported age breakdown lists ages 3, 4, and 5 only.
evidence_items.ambiguity: The extraction does not clarify whether the absence of a separately listed age-6 group reflects no age-6 participants or a reporting issue.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Data were collected in Fuyang City, Anhui Province, China, via the Wenjuanxing platform. All respondents were mothers.
evidence_items.population: Children aged 3 to 6 years and their mothers in Fuyang City, Anhui Province, China
evidence_items.causal_strength: Descriptive population information only.
evidence_items.limitation: The findings may not generalize beyond the sampled location, recruitment context, and mother-reported data.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The design was longitudinal, with three assessment waves labeled T1, T2, and T3. The waves were spaced four months apart.
evidence_items.numeric_scope: T1, T2, and T3
evidence_items.population: Study participants
evidence_items.date_or_period: Three assessment waves, each separated by 4 months; exact calendar dates are not provided
evidence_items.causal_strength: Temporal ordering supports longitudinal mediation analysis, but does not by itself establish causality.
evidence_items.limitation: The authors state that the study captures only a limited developmental time window and that the relatively short measurement interval may not reflect the dynamic interplay over longer periods.
evidence_items.source_location: Study Design; Time Points; Stated Limitations

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Parent–child relationship was measured with the Chinese revised version of the Child-Parent Relationship Scale (CPRS), revised by Deng (2013). It contained a Closeness subscale with 7 items and a Conflict subscale with 8 items, using a five-point Likert scale from 1 (not at all true) to 5 (completely true). Internal consistency was alpha=0.882 for Closeness and alpha=0.895 for Conflict.
evidence_items.numeric_value: Closeness: 7 items, alpha=0.882; Conflict: 8 items, alpha=0.895; 5-point scale
evidence_items.numeric_scope: CPRS Chinese revised version
evidence_items.population: Parent–child relationship reports in the study
evidence_items.causal_strength: Measurement description; reliability coefficients indicate internal consistency but do not establish causal validity.
evidence_items.limitation: All core variables were reported by a single informant.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Screen time was measured with two items asking about average daily electronic-device use on weekdays and weekends. A weighted daily average was calculated as (weekday average × 5 + weekend average × 2) / 7.
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Average daily electronic-device use
evidence_items.population: Children in the study
evidence_items.causal_strength: Measurement description only.
evidence_items.limitation: The authors state that the screen-time measure does not capture important contextual information that may be critical for understanding its role in child development.
evidence_items.ambiguity: The extraction does not specify the response units or provide details about device types, content, or usage context.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Behavioral problems were measured with the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Externalizing problems used Hyperactivity/Inattention and Conduct Problems subscales, each with 5 items, with alpha=0.891. Internalizing problems used Emotional Symptoms and Peer Problems subscales, each with 5 items, with alpha=0.853. Items used a three-point scale from 1 (not true) to 3 (certainly true).
evidence_items.numeric_value: Externalizing alpha=0.891; Internalizing alpha=0.853; 5 items per component subscale; 3-point scale
evidence_items.numeric_scope: SDQ externalizing and internalizing problem measures
evidence_items.population: Children in the study
evidence_items.causal_strength: Measurement description; reliability coefficients indicate internal consistency but do not establish causal validity.
evidence_items.limitation: All core variables were reported by a single informant, and the extraction identifies the respondents as mothers.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Higher conflictual parent–child relationship at T1 was associated with higher internalizing behavioral problems at T3: beta=0.476, p<0.001, 95% CI [0.302, 0.650].
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 主な統計結果：ConflictからInternalizingへの関連
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Conflictual parent–child relationship T1 to internalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Longitudinal association; not proof of a causal effect.
evidence_items.limitation: The study did not include baseline levels of key variables, so the association may partly reflect pre-existing levels of the constructs.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Higher conflictual parent–child relationship at T1 was associated with higher externalizing behavioral problems at T3: beta=0.273, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.118, 0.428].
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 主な統計結果：ConflictからExternalizingへの関連
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Conflictual parent–child relationship T1 to externalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Longitudinal association; not proof of a causal effect.
evidence_items.limitation: Stable between-person differences at initial assessment were not controlled through baseline levels of key variables.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Higher conflictual parent–child relationship at T1 was associated with greater screen time at T2: beta=0.208, p<0.001, 95% CI [0.094, 0.322].
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 主な統計結果：Conflictからscreen timeへの関連
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Conflictual parent–child relationship T1 to screen time T2
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Longitudinal association consistent with the proposed mediation sequence; not proof of causality.
evidence_items.limitation: The screen-time measure lacks contextual information, and baseline levels of key variables were not included.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Greater screen time at T2 was associated with higher internalizing problems at T3: beta=0.148, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.011, 0.285].
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 主な統計結果：screen timeからInternalizingへの関連
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Screen time T2 to internalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Longitudinal association; not proof that screen time causes internalizing problems.
evidence_items.limitation: The screen-time measure does not capture contextual information, and the authors caution about causal implications.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Greater screen time at T2 was associated with higher externalizing problems at T3: beta=0.149, p<0.05, 95% CI [0.016, 0.282].
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 主な統計結果：screen timeからExternalizingへの関連
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Screen time T2 to externalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Longitudinal association; not proof that screen time causes externalizing problems.
evidence_items.limitation: The screen-time measure does not capture contextual information, and the authors caution about causal implications.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The reported indirect effect of conflictual parent–child relationship through screen time on internalizing problems was beta=0.031, p<0.05, 95% CI [-0.026, 0.088].
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Conflict T1 → screen time T2 → internalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Reported indirect association in a longitudinal mediation model; authors explicitly caution about causal implications.
evidence_items.limitation: Baseline levels of key variables were not included; other mediating or moderating pathways may exist.
evidence_items.ambiguity: The reported p-value is below 0.05, while the stated 95% CI includes zero; this apparent inconsistency should be preserved and checked in the original article or statistical output.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The reported indirect effect of conflictual parent–child relationship through screen time on externalizing problems was beta=0.031, p<0.05, 95% CI [-0.022, 0.084].
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Conflict T1 → screen time T2 → externalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Reported indirect association in a longitudinal mediation model; authors explicitly caution about causal implications.
evidence_items.limitation: Baseline levels of key variables were not included; other mediating or moderating pathways may exist.
evidence_items.ambiguity: The reported p-value is below 0.05, while the stated 95% CI includes zero; this apparent inconsistency should be preserved and checked in the original article or statistical output.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Closeness at T1 was not significantly associated with screen time at T2: beta=0.006, p>0.05, 95% CI [-0.088, 0.100].
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 主な統計結果：Closenessからscreen timeへの関連
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Close parent–child relationship T1 to screen time T2
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: No statistically significant longitudinal association was reported.
evidence_items.limitation: A null association in this study does not establish that closeness has no effect in other populations or contexts.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Greater closeness at T1 was associated with lower internalizing problems at T3: beta=-0.157, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.294, -0.020].
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 主な統計結果：ClosenessからInternalizingへの関連
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Close parent–child relationship T1 to internalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Longitudinal association; not proof of a causal protective effect.
evidence_items.limitation: Baseline levels of key variables were not included, and all core variables came from a single informant.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Greater closeness at T1 was associated with lower externalizing problems at T3: beta=-0.213, p<0.001, 95% CI [-0.346, -0.080].
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 主な統計結果：ClosenessからExternalizingへの関連
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Close parent–child relationship T1 to externalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: Longitudinal association; not proof of a causal protective effect.
evidence_items.limitation: Baseline levels of key variables were not included, and all core variables came from a single informant.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Indirect effects of closeness through screen time were reported as not significant for either internalizing or externalizing problems.
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 媒介効果：Closeness経由の間接効果
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Close relationship T1 → screen time T2 → internalizing or externalizing problems T3
evidence_items.population: Study sample of children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.causal_strength: The reported mediation paths were not statistically significant; causal mediation should not be inferred.
evidence_items.limitation: The authors state that parent–child relationship associations may operate through more complex mechanisms and other mediators or moderators.
evidence_items.ambiguity: The extraction does not provide coefficients, p-values, or confidence intervals for these nonsignificant indirect effects.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The reported model fit indices were chi-square(7)=19.27, p<0.05; RMSEA=0.057 with 90% CI [0.028, 0.089]; CFI=0.950; TLI=0.917; and SRMR=0.028.
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Reported mediation/model fit
evidence_items.population: Study sample
evidence_items.causal_strength: Model fit statistics describe correspondence between the reported model and the data; they do not establish causality.
evidence_items.limitation: The extraction does not specify the estimation method or provide additional model specification details.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The study did not include baseline levels of key variables, which may leave stable between-person differences insufficiently controlled. The authors state that some observed indirect effects may partly reflect pre-existing construct levels rather than purely developmental processes.
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Interpretation of longitudinal and indirect effects
evidence_items.population: Study participants
evidence_items.causal_strength: Explicit author caution against interpreting the mediation findings as purely developmental or causal.
evidence_items.limitation: No baseline levels of key variables were included.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The authors caution that the association between parent–child relationships and children’s behavioral outcomes does not necessarily operate directly through screen time. Other indirect pathways and moderating processes may be involved.
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Proposed mediation mechanism
evidence_items.population: Children in the study
evidence_items.causal_strength: The authors explicitly state that the observed association should not be interpreted as demonstrating a unique or complete screen-time pathway.
evidence_items.limitation: The model may omit other mediators or moderators.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The authors explicitly state that caution is warranted when interpreting the causal implications of the observed mediating effects.
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Observed mediating effects
evidence_items.population: Study participants
evidence_items.causal_strength: Direct author statement limiting causal interpretation.
evidence_items.limitation: The study is longitudinal but observational as described in the extraction; longitudinal ordering alone does not establish causation.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The screen-time measure does not capture important contextual information that may be critical for understanding its role in child development.
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Screen-time measurement
evidence_items.population: Children in the study
evidence_items.causal_strength: This limitation reduces interpretability of the screen-time associations and mediation results.
evidence_items.limitation: No contextual information is captured by the reported two-item measure.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: All core variables were reported by a single informant, and reliance on a single information source was identified as a methodological limitation.
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 測定上の限界・common informant limitation
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Parent–child relationship, screen time, and behavioral-problem variables
evidence_items.population: All study participants
evidence_items.causal_strength: Single-informant reporting may limit confidence in associations but does not by itself determine their direction or causality.
evidence_items.limitation: The extraction identifies all respondents as mothers, so the core variables were mother-reported.

evidence_items.evidence_summary: The study covers only a limited developmental time window. The relatively short measurement interval may not adequately capture the dynamic interplay among screen time, parent–child relationships, and behavioral problems over time.
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Developmental follow-up period
evidence_items.population: Children aged 3 to 6 years
evidence_items.date_or_period: Limited developmental time window; exact total duration is not stated beyond three waves 4 months apart
evidence_items.causal_strength: The limitation constrains claims about longer-term developmental processes.
evidence_items.limitation: Generalizability across longer developmental periods should be interpreted with caution.
evidence_items.source_location: Time Points; Stated Limitations, fourth bullet

evidence_items.evidence_summary: Although participants were recruited through kindergartens and classes, the study did not explicitly model the nested data structure, such as children within classes or schools. Potential clustering effects therefore cannot be entirely ruled out.
evidence_items.supported_fact_category: 統計モデル・一般化の限界
evidence_items.numeric_scope: Data structure and model specification
evidence_items.population: Children recruited through kindergartens and classes
evidence_items.causal_strength: Unmodeled clustering may affect standard errors and interpretation of estimated associations.
evidence_items.limitation: Potential class- or school-level clustering was not explicitly modeled.
